meta.title: Identification of the Gravitational Constant from Satellite Trajectories Using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations

abstract: The rapid growth of satellite constellations in low Earth orbit has increased the probability of collisions involving satellites and debris, making accurate orbit propagation increasingly important. However, accurate orbit prediction remains challenging. Propagators depend on spacecraft properties, environmental parameters, and nonconservative forces that are often uncertain, causing propagation errors to accumulate over time. Estimating these values directly from orbital data offers a solution that could improve propagation accuracy. This work investigates whether a global physical constant can be identified directly from real orbital data using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs). A hybrid Neural ODE model is developed in which the equations of motion of satellites are split into two parts: known gravitational dynamics, with the gravitational constant treated as a trainable parameter, and a Neural Network that learns the residual accelerations representing the unmodelled forces. Using different initial biases, the model successfully recovers the gravitational constant for relative errors of up to 150%. Increasing the initialization error primarily increases the number of training epochs required for convergence, as the final relative errors achieved are below 0.02% for all different initial biases used. At higher initial errors, the Neural Network instead compensates for the incorrect gravitational term by learning residual accelerations several orders of magnitude larger than physically expected, preventing recovery of the gravitational constant. These results show that Neural ODEs can recover physical parameters from real orbital data, while also revealing the limits of parameter identifiability when unknown dynamics are learned simultaneously.

blocks.html: Over the last four years, the number of active satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) has increased by 431%, from 2 548 satellites on 15 July 2022 to 13 541 satellites on 6 February 2026. The primary contributor to this growth is the Starlink constellation, which currently accounts for approximately 70% of all active satellites in LEO, according to data from Celestrak. This rapid increase in the number of active satellites in orbit raises concerns about potential collisions between Resident space objects (RSO). Although a collision between satellites has not happened since 2009, thousands of trackable fragments from it are still present in LEO and will be for the next 100 years [1] [2]. These fragments increase conjunction rates, as satellites must now avoid both operational spacecraft and debris. As a result, precise orbit propagation is more critical than ever for ensuring safe operations and long-term sustainability in LEO. However, predicting orbits is made more complicated given the stochasticity of the non-conservative forces acting on the satellites and the lack of information about them.

Classical numerical and analytical orbit propagation methods rely on explicitly defined dynamical models, where the governing equations and their associated parameters are assumed to be known. In practice, this assumption is often incorrect as information about the satellites themselves may be unavailable as well as the force model parameters. A promising approach to address this limitation is the use of data-driven methods to extract the missing information directly from the data. However, because orbital data is inherently noisy, isolating and recovering these parameters from measurements becomes challenging.

Analytical and numerical approaches to orbit propagation rely on simplified force models and approximations of the RSO and environmental parameters in order to solve the equations of motion or simulate the space environment. Even widely used methods like the Simplified General Perturbations 4 (SGP4) model, developed in 1970, are based on simplified representations of the system dynamics which causes their accuracy to degrade over time as errors accumulate [3] [4] [5].

Machine learning has been used for orbit propagation to compensate for these limitations by learning and correcting the residual errors of traditional propagators rather than replacing them entirely [6]. Work by H. Peng et al. explored techniques such as Support Vector Machines and Artificial Neural Networks to reduce prediction errors from SGP4, showing that data-driven post-processing can reduce propagation inaccuracies [6] [7] [8] [9].

Fully data-driven approaches to orbit propagation have emerged as alternatives to these hybrid correction schemes. These methods are able to infer the dynamics of the system directly from the data, allowing the models to rely less on knowledge of the forces acting on satellites and information about them. From the various machine learning models available, physics-informed approaches, like Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs), stand out for explicitly incorporating the physics of the orbital motion into the training process through the differential equation of motion of the satellites [10] [11]. The main distinction between PINNs and Neural ODEs lies in how the differential equation is integrated into the model. In addition to solving the forward problem, these models also have the ability to discover missing parameters from the ODE, this is known as the inverse problem [12] [13]. These parameters can be learned from the data during training, allowing the model to infer governing quantities alongside the system dynamics.

Although PINNs incorporate physics into the model, they can suffer from numerical instabilities during backpropagation that complicate the optimization process. The addition of the differential operator in the loss can create an ill-conditioned loss landscape with large valleys and flat surfaces making optimizers stall in saddle points [14]. Moreover, the physics encoded into the model via the ODE is only enforced during training, which means the model can still produce predictions at inference time that do not follow the laws of physics. For these reasons, Neural Ordinary Differential Equations were adopted in this work over PINNs.

Neural Ordinary Differential Equations [11] incorporate the system dynamics by representing the right-hand side of the ordinary differential equation with a Neural Network. The model defines a continuous transformation of the input over time:
where fNN is the Neural Network with parameters θ, dependent on the state h(t) and time t.

The Neural Network models the system’s gradient vector field, outputting the time derivatives of the state at the time requested. These derivatives are integrated by a numerical ODE solver, evolving the state over time by querying the Neural Network for gradient information as needed to approximate the solution to the Initial Value Problem (IVP):

blocks.html: where h(ti) is the initial state at time ti, h(tf) is the state at the final time tf. The ODE solver can be easily replaced with any of the solvers available in PyTorch, allowing for a trade off between computational efficiency and accuracy.

Backpropagation through the ODE solver, although possible, is costly and can introduce numerical errors. To address this, Chen et al. replaced standard backpropagation with the adjoint sensitivity method, treating the ODE solver as a black box. The adjoint sensitivity method computes the gradients of the loss by solving an augmented ODE using the adjoint variable:
The augmented ODE includes the system state, the adjoint variable, and the sensitivities of the loss:

The ODE solver can then compute these quantities at earlier times by integrating the augmented system backward in time. This process is equivalent to the backwards pass, and computes all the needed gradients for the model to learn and update its weights based on previous predictions, just like traditional backpropagation.

A limitation of the original Neural ODE formulation arises from the uniqueness of solutions guaranteed by the Picard–Lindelöf theorem when the vector field is Lipschitz continuous [15]. Under this condition, each initial state defines a single, non-intersecting trajectory, preventing different initial conditions from evolving to the same state at the same time. In Augmented Neural ODEs, the system is evolved in a higher-dimensional space where uniqueness is preserved, and the solution is then projected back to the original coordinates. This allows for more expressive dynamics in the observed space while maintaining a wellposed differential equation [16].

In contrast to prior literature that predominantly evaluates prediction accuracy or residual reduction, this work focuses on the conditions under which a global physical constant can be recovered from real, noisy orbital data when dynamics are only partially modeled and residual accelerations are learned jointly. We show that, even in the absence of complete system knowledge, accurate orbit propagation remains possible. This framework can subsequently be extended to infer additional unknown satellite characteristics directly from trajectory data, allowing for complete system modeling and therefore improving the accuracy of orbit propagation.

The data used in this parameter estimation problem belongs to real orbiting satellites from the Starlink megaconstellation. This data is made publicly available by SpaceX through SPACE-Track in the form of ephemerides files.

Ephemerides are tabular data containing the positions and velocities of celestial bodies, together with their associated covariance. For Starlink satellites, the ephemerides consist of three day predictions of these quantities provided in the Modified ITC format. A detailed description of this format is available in the Spaceflight Safety Handbook for Satellite Operators [17]. The data used for the tasks described in Section 4 consist of single orbit segments extracted from the full Starlink ephemerides. The data includes two satellite versions, v1 and v1.5, which operate in different orbital regimes and have different masses, introducing dynamical diversity into the dataset.
This paper uses Neural ODEs to solve two different inverse problems and a subsequent forward prediction task:
• Parameter estimation: the model estimates an unknown physical parameter of the governing ordinary differential equation;
• System identification: the model learns unknown components of the dynamics through trainable model weights;
• System propagation: the model propagates the system state forward in time.
The two inverse tasks lead to the dynamics of the satellites being expressed as:

blocks.html: where fphysics represents the known physical acceleration dependent on the gravitational constant to be estimated G, and fNN is the Neural Network with parameters θ that captures the unknown accelerations. The known physical acceleration is given by the two-body model with the J2 and J3 corrections:
where M is the Earth’s mass, assumed known.

The gravitational constant G is treated as a trainable scalar parameter while the network learns the unknown physics. The Neural Network parameters θ are learned jointly with G by minimizing trajectory prediction error after numerical integration of the system. An overview of the model architecture is shown in Figure 1.

The Neural Network outputs the time derivatives of the position, dr/dt, and velocity, dv/dt, at the requested time t, and estimates the gravitational constant, completing the right-hand side of Equation (5). In order to do so, the Neural Network only needs to predict the derivative of the velocity, as the derivative of position can be set to be equal to the velocity. This allows the network to require less parameters to learn the ODE, as it only needs to output three values, instead of six.

The resulting system of differential equations is integrated using a numerical integrator to propagate the trajectory forward in time from the initial conditions. During integration, the numerical solver queries the Neural Network for the gradient information at each integration step, as described in Section 2.1.

Together with the fixed J2 and J3 corrections these form dv/dt, while dr/dt = v. A numerical solver integrates the state, querying the network at each step, to produce the predicted trajectory. The gravitational constant G is treated as a trainable parameter of the network, initialized with a relative bias.

blocks.html: In a scenario where all the forces acting on the satellite are known, the problem is simplified to the parameter estimation task. However, because the data used to train the model is derived from observations of real satellites, the acting forces are partially unknown. As such these unknown forces must be estimated using a Neural Network.

The model updates both the Neural Network parameters and the gravitational constant G once per epoch, after accumulating gradients over all training orbits. This choice is motivated by the fact that G is a global parameter shared across all orbits, and therefore its update should reflect all the training orbits rather than individual trajectories. Updating G on a per-orbit basis would lead to gradients computed under progressively changing model parameters, resulting in the gradient being pulled in several directions. To maintain coherence between the optimization of G and the Neural Network weights, both are updated jointly at the epoch level using the aggregated gradient over all orbits. Given this, the loss function is defined as:

blocks.html: where Norb is the number of orbits. The epoch level loss is the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the model predictions, ˆhi(tij; G, θ), of the position and velocity vectors, h(t) = [r(t), v(t)]⊤∈R6, using the predicted G and the real trajectory, hi(tij):

The Neural ODE models were trained on Starlink ephemerides described in Section 3, with the gravitational constant initialized at varying offsets from its true value to test the limits of parameter recovery. We evaluate whether G can be identified from trajectory data alone, and under what conditions the optimization fails. Table 1 summarizes the recovery of the gravitational constant across initialization conditions. The model successfully recovers the true value of G = 6.674 × 10−11 m3 kg−1 s−2 for initial errors up to 150%, with final errors below 0.02% in all successful cases. Larger initial errors require more epochs to converge, 154 epochs at 10% versus 198 at 150%, showing that the optimization problem becomes harder as the starting point moves further from the true value.

blocks.html: The two-body force dominates satellite dynamics in LEO, therefore errors in G propagate directly into position errors. When the model successfully recovers the gravitational constant, this coupling is visible throughout training, Figure 2 shows that the position RMSE and the relative error in G decrease and increase together, confirming that correcting G is the primary driver of prediction accuracy. Recovery fails at 200% initial error, as seen in Figure 3, the model converges to an error of 99%, G = 3.65 × 10−14 m3 kg−1 s−2, yet the trajectory loss continues to decrease. The Neural Network compensates by inflating its learned accelerations to 2.4 × 10−3 km/s2, roughly one third of the two-body gravitational acceleration at 550 km altitude. The expected learned acceleration from the model corresponds to the accumulation of all forces acting on satellites except the two-body term. Therefore the learned residual acceleration should be of the same order of magnitude as the dominant non-gravitational perturbation, which for LEO satellites is atmospheric drag. The learned acceleration is six orders of magnitude larger than the expected residual acceleration from drag (∼10−9 km/s2, estimated using NRLMSISE-00 [18]), confirming that the network is absorbing the gravitational error rather than learning residual physics from other forces. When convergence occurs, the learned acceleration decreases with the error in the gravitational constant, as shown in Figure 4. During training, the predicted value of G initially oscillates around the true value as the optimization adjusts both the Neural Network parameters and the physical constant. As training progresses, the mean oscillations decrease and the estimate converges to 6.6746 × 10−11 m3 kg−1 s−2.

blocks.html: The results from this work show that Neural ODEs can recover the gravitational constant to within 0.02% for initial biases up to 150%, even when residual dynamics are learned jointly from noisy orbital data. Convergence requires more epochs as the initial error increases, however the final accuracy remains consistent for all runs. Initial errors of 200% define an identifiability boundary as the model is not able to learn the value of G, finding it easier to absorb the error in the accelerations than correct G. Future work could extend this work to recover unknown parameters such as drag coefficients or atmospheric density, allowing for more complete system identification from trajectory data alone.

This work presents learning-based methods for inferring physical parameters from satellite trajectory data using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, with the aim of improving the accuracy of orbit modeling and prediction. The study relies exclusively on publicly available orbital ephemerides and does not involve personal or sensitive data. Improved orbit determination can contribute to safer satellite operations and more reliable conjunction assessment.
